utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Today, I would like to ask for appearances, because if I'm not mistaken, we have the first time you as the representative of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and everybody. My name is Rupert Elderkin, and I'm appearing this morning with Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Stewart on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the Defence is the same as always. Before we start with the witness, at the outset of our hearing of today, the Chamber would like to deal with four procedural matters. The first one is the following: During the examination of Witness Ruez last week, the parties were using material provided by a state pursuant to Rule 70 of our Rules. The Chamber noticed that the Prosecution was referring to specific conditions of the provider under which the Prosecution may present this material. The Prosecutor explicitly stated that the Defence had been provided with letters of agreement about this material. However, the Chamber was not notified of such letters. Thus, the Chamber is not in a position to decide if a specific question by either party goes beyond the scope of Rule 70. The Chamber, therefore, requests the Prosecution, firstly, to indicate to the Trial Chamber which material currently the Rule 65 ter exhibit list was provided to them pursuant to Rule 70; and, secondly, to provide the Chamber with a statement of conditions under which the Prosecution may present this material. This could avoid some conflicts and discussions during the evidence of the witness. The second point. The Chamber noticed that the exhibited transcripts of prior testimonies are not yet replaced by corrected and official transcripts, as requested by the Chamber. We would like to remind the Prosecution to do that as soon as possible and to bear that obligation in mind in relation to future 92 ter witnesses. The third point is the following: Yesterday, the Chamber received two urgent Prosecution motions. The first one is the urgent Prosecution motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list, to add documents relating to Dusan Janc's updated report filed yesterday. In this motion, the Prosecution urgently requests to add material to its 65 ter exhibit list. Now the Chamber invites the Defence to make oral submissions in relation to this motion. Mr. Tolimir, do you want to address the Chamber on this topic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Praise the Lord to everyone, and I would like to have this trial completed according to God's will. I have received some notification from the Prosecution in English, but it hasn't been translated, that to me, that they wish to admit some documents. If the Trial Chamber has seen the majority of the documents, and the Defence hasn't seen them, I believe that the Defence has full trust in the view of the Chamber regarding those documents, so that can also then apply to the position of the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Does the Prosecution want to respond to that? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. No, we've been in discussions with Mr. Gajic about this and have been trying to get this -- get any materials that need be translated and worked out with them so this witness can be put on and the material used. And, of course, we remain flexible on this if there are any serious issues, but we're all -- both planning on dealing with Mr. Janc. And if there are any serious issues, we'll remain flexible on that, of course. But given the small amount and the fact that most -- the vast majority of Mr. Janc's report is the old report, we didn't think there is a problem, and we hope there isn't. But, as I said, we, of course, remain flexible if there's any serious issue the Defence had. We haven't heard it thus far, but we are in discussions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The Chamber is inclined to grant leave to add these documents to the 65 ter list. However, if you want to use these documents during examination-in-chief of the witness Dusan Janc, in that case perhaps we have to postpone the finalisation of the examination-in-chief to give the Defence the opportunity to review these documents and to prepare the cross-examination. I don't know what you have in mind about the use of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we -- well, we wanted to use them, we wanted the Court to be able to see them, and we're open to any flexible resolution like that. It is fine with us, and we can discuss any particular documents with the Defence and see if there's anything we can do to get around the problem. Mr. Thayer has been talking mostly with Mr. Gajic, and as far as I know they are moving forward, but discussions continue as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think both parties should discuss this problem during the next break and during the hearing of today to find a way to deal with this problem. Therefore, at the moment there is no decision needed. My fourth point is the second motion, the urgent Prosecution motion for leave to supplement its Rule 92 ter materials for the witness scheduled for today, also filed confidentially yesterday. The Prosecution's intention appears to be that these exhibits should be marked for identification now so that they can be admitted with another witness later. It would only be at that point that strictly the 92 ter statements of the witness would be fully comprehensible. It would be not satisfactory that a 92 ter statement should not be fully comprehensible when the witness concerned is called to testify. The Chamber would like to ask the Prosecution how, if the exhibits are not admitted, they can assist the Trial Chamber to see the two documents in order to make sense of the transcript. We presume that the Prosecution has not sought the admission of the exhibits because it realises that it would be seeking this at an unacceptably late stage. It appears that it did not seek the admission of the exhibits in the first 92 ter motion of the 18th of March, 2009. The Chamber invites the Defence again to make oral submissions in relation to this motion. Mr. Tolimir, do you want to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My legal advisor has advised me that he is acquainted with the matter, up to a point. And if the Prosecution does not intend to tender those documents into evidence, then we can accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you want to respond? Please, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, if I may. The motion was filed at a very late stage simply based on our re-review of the proposed 92 ter statement and also, as Your Honours will see in the motion, based on our understanding of the requirements of the March 30th decision. To cut it short, the two documents in question are the standard-format vehicle logs, the same as a third document which is on the witness's list of exhibits for today, for which we would seek admission, and the discussion of the two other documents simply explains the format of the standard form. And because one document rather than the other was used for that explanation, we wanted to make sure that it would assist Your Honours, that it be available to be seen. We don't consider substantively that its content is necessary to explain the witness's evidence, other than for that reason. And, therefore, based on the disposition of the 30th of March decision, we understood that we should be identifying those, but we don't seek their admission either now or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As you will be aware, this is the concern of the Chamber. If you wanted to have it with the transcript of the witness's evidence, to have a full picture of his evidence, I think in that case you should tender these documents. Because of the importance of the exhibits for an understanding of the testimony of the witness, the Prosecution will be allowed to make use of them, as requested in the motion. However, the Prosecution should consider to tender these documents as exhibits with this witness and should have brought them to the attention of the Chamber much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the Registrar would like to read something for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Considering that on Wednesday, 12th of May, 2010, the Prosecution provided the Registry with the 65 ter numbers for the testimony and exhibits related to Witness PW-068, as ordered by the Trial Chamber in its 30th March, 2010, decision on Prosecution's motion regarding Rule 65 ter witness and exhibit lists, Rule 92 ter, and protective measures. And pursuant to such decision, the Registry has marked for identification such documents as follows: 65 ter 06239, the OTP interview statement of Witness PW-068, is now P155, marked for identification and under seal. 65 ter 06240, the sketch made during the interview, is now Exhibit P156, marked for identification and under seal. 65 ter 05752 is now P157, marked for identification and under seal. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now the witness should be brought in, but first we should close the windows to enable the witness to come in, in a protected way. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if the request has been passed up, but in the previous trial this witness appeared, he was given a caution concerning conditions of Rule 90(E), and I would request that Your Honours give the same caution in this case, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is our understanding, that face and voice distortion will be provided to the witness, and addressed only by pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in addition to the protective measures, the witness, given his -- given his position, the nature of his evidence, is a person who may be in a position where he may have to answer questions that might tend to incriminate him, and for that reason, certainly, we've seen practice in the past, which may be reflected by Your Honours, that a witness is warned of this provision and equally warned and cautioned that if compelled to answer those questions, the answers may not be used against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please read allowed the affirmation to tell the truth, which is shown on the card to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that. The interpreters didn't hear you. It was too silent or the microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone is far away, but I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Sir, before the Prosecutor starts with his questioning, I would like to tell you two things. The first is we are aware of the fact that you are perhaps not very well and you need a break. If that is the case, please indicate immediately so that we can have a break then and you can recover. The second point is I would like to read out one Rule of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence - this is Rule 90(E) - so that you will be aware of your rights. It states: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." I hope you will be aware of this legal situation. Now Mr. Elderkin has some questions for you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. As you know, my name is Rupert Elderkin, and before we get started I just want to remind you to try to keep your voice up and to speak a little slowly so that the interpreters will be able to translate what we are saying. And if there's anything that I ask of you that's unclear, please let me know, and I'll do my best to rephrase the question. Can I ask that the witness please be shown the pseudonym sheet, which is 65 ter 6238. Sir, please, could you look at the screen in front of you. And without saying aloud what is written there, can you confirm if that is your name on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I would ask to tender that under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P158, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall making a statement to the Prosecution on the 15th of March, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read that statement yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And are there two small corrections which should be made to that statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please, could we see the statement, which is 65 ter 6239, and also should not be broadcast. And if we could go to page 38 in the B/C/S, and page 37 is the corresponding page in the English. And in the B/C/S, if we could zoom in, as best as possible, to see around line 12, and the English at around line 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, should the word "kamionu" in B/C/S at line 12 instead read "minibus"?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we please now could go to page 40 in the B/C/S, right at the bottom of that page, and English at page 39, around line 28, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, I'm not sure if we had the right page on the screen before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I'm sorry. Is Your Honour referring to my reference to "kamionu," that page, or the one we've moved to now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, we don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what is showing up on everyone else's screens, but we seem to have got a lopped page on both sides, so I can't see the relevant page numbering at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I'll go back to the first one, just to make sure everyone is clear. So it was at B/C/S page 38 and English page 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Well, the B/C/S line would be line 12, and the English line 7. However, I'm not seeing the corresponding text on the screen here. That's correct now. The B/C/S is correct. The English still needs to be taken, please, to page 37. And the English would be at line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, if I may ask again, should the word "kamionu" at line 12 in the B/C/S instead say "minibus"?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to the second correction, which is page 40 in the B/C/S, so two pages further on, and at page 39 in the English, also two pages further on, please. And it will be towards bottom of both pages, so lines 31 to 33 in the B/C/S, and line 28 in the English. Sir, at lines 32 to 33, should the reference to "Daco or Dule" be corrected to "Dule or Dusan"?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: They called him Dule. I don't know if his name is Dusan or not, but they called him Dule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Noting these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, just a moment. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the transcript that I see on the screen, it says his nickname is Dugme, not Dule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, noting the two corrections that you have made, does this statement fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Sir, considering the two corrections that you've just indicated, apart from these, does your statement fairly and accurately reflect your answers if you were asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask now to have the statement admitted under seal, along with the attached sketch which is currently listed as 65 ter 6240. And we just got the numbers for those, which are P155 for the statement and P156 for the sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, could you please indicate what is the content of this sketch so that we have an idea of what we receive?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could call up, please, 65 ter 6240, and it perhaps best not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the drawing in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could please scroll down to see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The transcript will be an exhibit under seal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and the sketch, which is already marked for identification, as I was told, will be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, I'd like to read now a very short summary of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. We need the number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement is now Exhibit P155. The sketch will be Exhibit P156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And both under seal, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And with permission, I would like to read a very short summary of the witness's evidence, and this can be in open session. The witness was a driver for the VRS. On the 23rd of July of 1995, he was ordered to drive a minibus. He collected a group of soldiers from their base in Dragasevac and drove them to Bisina. At Bisina, the soldiers left the minibus, and returned some hours later. The witness then drove them back to Dragasevac. The witness recorded in the vehicle log that the trip was authorised by Drina Corps security officer Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. That's my statement -- that's my summary, rather, Your Honours. I would ask if I may have permission to put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 5752, which should not be broadcast. And is it possible to scroll over to the right-hand side of the B/C/S? Thank you. And perhaps the same in the English, if we could zoom in on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: This is a travel order or vehicle work log.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: For what kind of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: For a minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Does your name appear anywhere on this page?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, please, could we see the second page both in the English and the B/C/S. And this time if we could scroll, please, to the left-hand side of those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you see your handwriting anywhere on this page?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you say which entries are your handwriting, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a little? From the 19th until the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is your journey to Bisina on the 23rd of July recorded here?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would ask now for the log to be admitted, also under seal. And we were already given the MFI number for that as P157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received as an exhibit, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's P157, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I understand correctly, I may go ahead and use the two documents discussed in the decision earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could see, please, 65 ter 6275, please. Your Honour, I'm not sure if this is available in English. And, again, if we could please zoom in on the right-hand side of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Vehicle work log.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you see your name anywhere on this page?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what vehicle is this log for, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that this be admitted, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P159, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we may now see, please, 65 ter 6276. Also, it should not be broadcast, please. And if we could see the right-hand half of the page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, what is this document, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Also a vehicle work log.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for what vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: A minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And does your name appear on this page, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I would ask for the admission also of this log, again under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation into English. And the same will be done with the previous document, only marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P160, marked for identification, under seal. And the same goes for P159, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. And thank you, Witness. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Sir, you know now Mr. Tolimir has the right to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Good day, Witness. I want to tell the witness I'm not going to say anything that would identify him. I know he's a protected witness. And if I ask something that could identify him, then he should not answer such questions, because he knows best how to protect himself, which is obvious from the statement he gave to the Prosecution. Witness, I don't have many questions for you, but I do want to ask you something about that interview you have given and the questions asked of you at the time by the people who were interviewing you. Do you know where the football stadium is in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the month of July, did you have occasion to go to Konjevic Polje, and did you drive Muslims there? I mean Muslim prisoners.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I did have occasion to go there, but not to drive Muslim prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 06239, which was on the screen a moment ago. That's the interview of this witness, page 31 and 33.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, that is P155, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I still cannot see the Serbian on the screen, but it's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We are looking at page 33 in the Serbian language, and in English it's also 33. In English, it's lines 1 through 5, and in Serbian, it starts at line 33 and then continues on page 34. Do you see this in front of you? I will read it out to you if you can't see well enough to read. It says -- the Prosecution says, at line 33: "We interviewed many people, including about Bisina. We have intercepts of conversations in the Drina Corps concerning Bisina. We know about the mass grave. We have been there. We know who dug out those graves, and we know that some of those people were alive before 23rd July. We know that they were taken there, that they were Muslim prisoners who were killed there on that day, and we know that the trucks of the Drina Corps went there to drive prisoners. And we know you went there with a minibus at the same time, on the same day. We know who the other people there were. That means you were sent to the Drina Corps like a punishment. We know you didn't want to be involved in this war. You only wanted to put bread on the table for your family. You told us you did not have weapons, you were not armed, and I believe from this conversation so far, from this interview, that you were not involved. We know you did not shoot at Bisina, but we know you drove people there and that you know what happened there, so we want you to tell us, in your own words, where you went, what you saw, what you heard, and what you remember." Were you able, Witness, to follow what I was reading aloud or to follow on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I did not make a statement as it is written here. I did drive people there, but I did not drive Muslim prisoners, nor did I see any trucks, nor did I see anything during those days, because I was in the rear, dealing with other problems such as supplies. On one of those days, on the 23rd, I was on a field mission, and when I returned, I got orders from my superior that our defence line was broken somewhere at Bisina and that I should drive a group of people who were waiting for me on the road near Vlasenica in a place called Dragasevac. My commander told me, Get out there and do it. I turned around and I went on the road to Sekovici. Indeed, there were some people standing next to some burned-down houses. They got onto the vehicle and they told me to change direction and not go to the command but towards Bisina. When we got there, to a point where the road was no longer good and I couldn't go on, they got out, and I stood there for about 15 minutes. An older man in an ordinary soldier's uniform came up to me and took me back -- perhaps a kilometre back; I can't be precise. There was the body of water there, something. I washed my face. People were building something there, perhaps barracks. Anyway, I had a drink of water. A man who was minding his cattle there came up to me, and I asked him, What's going on, grandfather? He said, Muslim forces are attacking every day. Our defence lines are broken. Don't ask. I was there for a couple of hours, all in all. It's all written in the vehicle work log. And suddenly they came. They were a bit dirty, tired. They got onto the vehicle, and I took them back to the same place on the road where I picked them up. That's what they wanted me to do, and that's what I did, and returned to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What I just read out is certainly not your words. Those were the words of the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor who interviewed you on the 15th of March, 2008, and he provided you with some broader information about these events. I only read it out to show how this interview was conducted. You just told us how you drove people there, and was this older man you mentioned a guard or something?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I did not manage to ask much within the five or ten minutes I was standing there. I couldn't turn around my minibus there. I had to go lower down towards a farm, and that's where I made a U-turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, based on the conversation you had with that older man who was a guard, who took you a kilometre and a half back, did you understand from him that the defence lines were broken?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you think that the people you took there were taken there in some connection with the fact that the lines were broken?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please display page 33 of this same document. Sorry, page 35, line 33 -- page 34 in Serbian, lines 25 and 26. In English, it is page 33, lines 24 to 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you can see here lines 25 to 27, and I can see it. I'm going to read to you what it says. I'm quoting what you said: "I didn't see anything. I didn't see them doing anything that they were not supposed to." Thank you, I have finished my quote. Does this refer to the people that you drove? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 64 now, lines 10 to 11. It's the same document. We are still seeing page 34 on the screen. Can we please look at page 64 in the Serbian version, lines 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor said to you: "We didn't say that you knew what your task would be." And then it says you say: "I couldn't say." There's a correction, actually, now, but in your original statement it said: "I couldn't say anything, yes or no. Had I seen anything, I would have said so, but I didn't see anything." This is what you say in lines 10-11 in the original transcript. And this is actually lines 26 and 27 in the Serbian. And in English, it's page 62, I'm being told by my legal advisor, lines 25 and 26.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Could you please put your question to me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm now reading lines 16 and 17. You can follow that on the screen: "I don't know, I didn't see it. I really couldn't say whether that did or didn't happen when I didn't. I wasn't there. Had I seen something, I would have said so. Had I seen it, I would have told about it, but I didn't." Are these your words?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And those who were putting the questions to you, did they believe you when you said that or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Well, you can ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Did you have the impression at the time that they believed what you were saying or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Well, I guess they did believe it if they put the question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they try to put the same question to you several times? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you must slow down a little bit and not overlap. It's very difficult for the interpreters. And then if you continue, please switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, I am going to show to you your statement 20 pages before what we have just read, and they're trying to convince you that you said something that you're saying you didn't. Now, we can look at page 43 of this interview. Let's go back from page 64 to page 43, lines 10, 11, and 12 in the Serbian version. Are you able to read lines 10, 11, 12 to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in on the text so it can be a little bit bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, another advice. When the witness is answering your questions, please switch off your microphone so that his voice can't be heard outside this courtroom. Thank you. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now switch on the mike.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's switched on. This is page 41 in English, lines 41 [as interpreted] to 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you can see what is being said 20 pages before this page 64, on page 43, lines 10 and 11: "No, no. Well, I have to be a little bit nervous, because you're wanting me to say something that I didn't see. I cannot say that. I could mention my brother, but I didn't see anything. I have children. I cannot. I am --" Witness, sir, will you please tell me whether this text that I read out, whether those are your words in your interview to the Prosecution on the 15th of March, 2008?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And is it evident that for a whole 20 pages, they're asking you to say something or talk about something that you didn't see? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you answer now whether that is some sort of pressure on you to say something that you didn't see?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I don't know if it is any kind of pressure. I'm not really well versed in such things in order to be able to explain something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we're going to look at page 49. Can we please look at page 49 in the Serbian version, lines 31 and 32. My legal advisor is going to see what page that is in the English version. In the Serbian, it is page 49, lines 31 and 32. The last sentence of that line, you are quoted as saying: "And please don't have me say something that I didn't see. I don't think that is fair." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, we have now seen, in these 20 pages, that the same matter is discussed. The Prosecution would like you to confirm the text that I read earlier, where you said you didn't see it, and now they want you to say what they want you to say, and you keep saying what I quoted you back as saying on these three pages. So my question is: Did you drive Muslim prisoners from Vlasenica to Bisina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is: Did you know where those people were going that you were driving from Vlasenica to Bisina, from their command at Dragasevac?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I don't know if their command is there, but I got an order from my chief to drive them up to the battalion command. The line was breached. And that was the whole quotation that I got from my boss. This is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. So you were driving in the hope that they would go and carry out a defence assignment in restoring breached lines; is that true?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Absolutely, this is what I was ordered. I don't know what they did, whether they went or not. This is not something that I was really was able to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Did you have the sense, when you were giving this interview in Belgrade on the 15th of March, 2008, which was attended by three or four people, that they would like you to produce a certain kind of statement, that they thought that you knew something that you actually don't know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to interfere in their work. What I knew, I told. As for everything else, I really couldn't say anything that I hadn't seen, so I couldn't give a statement like that, and I didn't. So that's that. I was just listening to the orders of my superior. Had I driven them, I would have said that, but as I didn't, I really couldn't say. I mean, I couldn't say that I did drive them if I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Well, just tell me, did they ask you whether you heard any firing from the location where you were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: They asked me, and there was shooting in the direction of the line, shooting, shelling, and so on. That is what you could hear even farther away, not only up to where I was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you. You have replied to my answers in accordance with the way you provided your statement. Thank you very much. May God bless you, and may you return home safely. Mr. President, I don't have any more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the name of the village outside Vlasenica where the 10th Sabotage Detachment was based?

utterances.speaker: PW-068
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can I note now that this was not the topic of the cross-examination and was not something that the witness mentioned in his statement. This goes outside of those two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, you heard the objection by Mr. Tolimir. You should bear in mind you should only deal with topics raised during cross-examination. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that question was related to Mr. Tolimir's reference to the command and the command where he picked people up from. So I don't have any further questions, based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a short question to put to you, but perhaps we should move to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Closed session, private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to know that this concludes the questioning for you. You may now return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and the assistance you could give us. Thank you very much again, and now you are free to leave the courtroom. But first the blinds will be brought down so that you will not be recognised out of the courtroom. Thank you very much again. The Court Officer will help you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can the blinds be brought up again, please. Good morning, Mr. Vanderpuye. I wonder if it would be a convenient time to have the break now so that everything can be prepared for the next witness, who has no protective measures, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you, Your Honours. That sounds like a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we will have our first break now, and we will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal. Could you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and please sit down. Mr. Vanderpuye has some questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning again. Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to you, Mr. Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you know, my name is Kweku Vanderpuye. We met yesterday, and I'm just going to put some questions to you regarding your evidence today. First, could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Nikodin Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovicic. Mr. Jovicic, do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor's investigators on 17 March 2008?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time you gave your statement, was it truthful?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity, prior to testifying here today, to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in reviewing the statement, did you read it yourself, or did you have it read back to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: I read it back myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you discuss that statement with me yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And other than the fact that you no longer work for the Han Pijesak police and that you do not personally know the circumstances surrounding the death of a person named Himzo Mujic's brother in 1992, does your statement fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. At this time, Your Honour, I would tender the witness's previous statement. It's 65 ter 6237.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P161, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a very brief summary of the witness's statement. It shouldn't take more than a minute or so. In July 1995, the witness was the deputy commander of the uniformed police in the Han Pijesak Police Station. The commander of the uniformed police at that time was Milan Perovic and Goran Kanostrevac, nicknamed Kane, served as chief of the police station. Prior to the war, Himzo Mujic, whom the witness described as a labourer from the Muslim village of Rijeka, worked for the witness as an operational contact. Mujic provided the witness with information concerning events in the Han Pijesak area. In mid-1992, the witness lost contact with Mujic. The witness read a 24 July 1995 intercept bearing the ERN number 0080-1169 through 0080-1174. In it, a Himzo Mujic is mentioned as seeking to talk to one Jovicic, as he used to work for him. The witness believes that the intercept refers to Mujic's attempt to reach the witness, in view of their pre-war working relationship. The witness did not have any information about Mujic's whereabouts or whether he tried to help Mujic in July 1995. However, he does not exclude that he may have done so. The witness also noticed the name Neso Rubez in the intercept. The witness new Nenad Rubez from elementary school in Han Pijesak and that in 1995 he was in the army doing office work. The witness, however, does not recall any conversation with Rubez or with Chief Goran Kanostrevac regarding Himzo Mujic. That concludes my summary of his statement, and I have just one or two questions for the witness. Witness, I'd like to show you very briefly the intercept that's referred to in your statement. That's 65 ter 3142A and 3142D. A is the English -- is the B/C/S; D is the English, please. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to read the handwritten intercept on the left side of your screen?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have an objection. The statement does not refer to this transcript anywhere. The witness is just asked whether he knew these two people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I take it Mr. Tolimir is referring to the statement. In the statement, this specific intercept is referred to. It's on paragraph 10. That's page 3 of the English statement, and I can locate it in the B/C/S so that it's clearer for Mr. Tolimir. But it's referred to specifically by ERN, as I read it into the record in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it's on page 3 in the B/C/S, and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the document is referred to, but there's nothing about the document in the statement, and there is nothing that is contained in the document that is quoted in the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how to respond to that. I can read the exact paragraph into the record, but I think it's really quite plain in the text of itself -- of the document itself. It reads as follows: "The investigator, Blaszczyk, showed me the document ERN 0080-1169 through 0080-1174, which I had an opportunity to read carefully. I was told that this transcript of an intercept from July 1995. In this document, the name Himzo Mujic is mentioned in the context that, 'He would like to talk to Jovicic because he used to work for him.' I believe that in this paragraph, Himzo Mujic is referring to me, having in mind that he cooperated with me before the war." Which is almost verbatim what my summary says, so I don't know exactly what Mr. Tolimir's objection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to this document, Mr. Jovicic, what I wanted to show you -- well, if we could just go through it a little bit. Right at the very beginning, you can see that this is a communication between Kane, X, and Y, extension 342, that's written at the very top of the intercept. And then you can see it starts off with X saying: "He was here at our place, I don't know if he still is, Himzo Mujic." That's on the first line. And Y responds: "That's what I'm calling you for, man." A few lines down, you can see the name Neso Rubez, as you've indicated in your statement, and then you can see that X says: "And, ah, he told him later on, over there, he said, 'I'd like to talk to Jovicic because I used to work for him.'" As we've just seen in his statement: "He worked for him and then the war started," was the response. And if we could go a little bit further down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, just for the record, I think you quoted correctly the B/C/S version. There is mention of Jovicic, and the English translation is only "Jovic" and not "Jovicic." That might be a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, how do you like that. You're right. I seem to have -- I do have a different document in front of me. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Actually, you know, the translation in front of you now indicates a time of 1135 hours, and it should indicate the time of 1132 hours, as you can see on the intercept on your left. And I think the translation that I have in front of me, which is 0091-2478 through 2479 is a translation of the handwritten intercept in front of you now, and what's on the screen is a translation of a print-out that was sent based on this intercept. In any event, I intend to offer all of this into evidence, so we can sort it out. Okay. Otherwise, I think substantively the intercept -- the translation is virtually identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we look further down the page, we can see here where X says: "I could try to call the warden, you know."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's in English and it's in the middle -- and it's in the middle of the page in the English translation. And I understand it's on page 2 of B/C/S, so if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S so the witness can follow. That's it there. It's the third -- basically, the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see that, Witness, where it says: "I could try to call the warden ..." And then it follows with: "Who is the warden?" And it says: "A guy named -- a guy called Dragic." That's at the bottom of the page in front of --

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then in page 2 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, you can see a reference to Himzo Mujic having been wounded in the leg. It says: "He's wounded. He said he needs a little treatment. He's wounded in the leg." And X responds: "No problem." Let me read the translation that you have in e-court so we're talking about the same thing. In e-court, it reads: "He's wounded. He said he needs a little treatment. He's wounded in the leg." And then it reads: "(Passage missing)" in parentheticals. But do you see that reference to Mr. Mujic being wounded in the leg in the B/C/S before you, the handwritten text?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in respect of Mr. Mujic being wounded in the leg, do you have any recollection of having discussed that with anyone at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, all right. That's all I have for you. I would like to tender this document into evidence; actually, all versions of it. Those consists of 3142, A through F; and 3143, A through D. Is that right? Just 3142 A through F, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, to have it clear on the record, it would be helpful if you could number the -- give the numbers of the documents again, but separately, and indicate if it's B/C/S and which one is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Okay. 3142A is B/C/S handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P162, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness had no knowledge about this document before he was interviewed by the Prosecution in 2008. It's only then that the Prosecutor read this out to him. At the time of the events, he had no knowledge about this document. I don't know how this can be admissible in this case, and the question is how this is being tendered, on what basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is now an exhibit. The Chamber ruled on that. And the witness was asked about the content of it, and his name was mentioned in it. And, therefore, the English translation will also be received, but please, Mr. Vanderpuye -- and, of course, you are in the position to ask questions during your cross-examination. Please, the number of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The number of the English translation is 3142B, as in "Boy." It's ERN 0091-2478 through 2479. That's the one I was reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This translation will be attached to the previous B/C/S exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Will you tender another English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The other English translation is 3142D, as in "David," and that is 0091-2476 through 2477, the ERN number. I believe that's the one that was displayed on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This one will be attached to the exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then there's another -- and then there's a print-out which attends to that translation, and that print-out is 0072-7930 through 0072-7931. The 65 ter number, I'm sorry, is 3142C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be a part of that exhibit as well, attached to that, so that we have a full picture of all versions of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then there's another print-out of the same intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To enable everybody to identify the documents properly, the last one you tendered will be a separate exhibit and will be received. This is 3142C.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President. I understand that we have some difficulty in terms of how to either keep these documents together or keep them apart, and the reason is that there are, in fact, a number of translations, a number of versions of these intercepts, which will become clearer to the Court once the interceptor operators actually arrive and start testifying about the process of taking these intercepts, which went from handwritten note-books, then were typed, transcribed, and then sent. So there are a number of versions of them. And, of course, I leave it to the Court's discretion as to how to organise them, but there are quite a number of them. I think there may be about 300 of them or so that we intend to tender into evidence, and with the attached translations, et cetera, it will be, I think, more than a thousand documents, or somewhere thereabouts. So I just want to let you know that it's going to get a lot worse. But for these purposes, there is one other print-out that I would like to tender as well, and the reason is there is a good version of the print-out, which is the 0320 series of documents, which I will explain if you'd like, and then there are the not-so-good print-outs, which are the 0072 versions of these documents, one of which I've already tendered at 3142C. So the one that I'd like to tender as well is 3142F, as in "Frank," and that is ERN 0320-5746 through 5747. That's a B/C/S print-out as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first time we are dealing with this problem of the best way. And later on, to be able to identify the specific document and translation, I think it will be received as an exhibit, but we will decide later and have to confer with the Registry which is the best way to have the numbering for later identification of all documents. But it will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all I have to tender in respect of this witness, and that completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Jovicic, you know now Mr. Tolimir has some questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to ask, all these documents that were referred to, because I couldn't follow and I was not able to see in different languages, in handwriting and typed up, are they all on this list of documents, the original list, or are they some other documents? Are they related to this witness? Can they be admitted through this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, they are all related to this witness. They all speak -- they all have the same content and the same text. They're simply different versions of this based on the handwritten document which was shown to the witness at 0080-1169 through 1174 that I referred to in the summary and in the statement itself. So they all have the same content, they all mentioned the same people, same circumstances. Everything is virtually identical between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, these are all part of the Prosecution exhibit list for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before we carry on, I think it could be helpful for everybody if you explain how it comes that there are different translations. What was the procedure which leads to this situation to have so many different documents? For the record and for a better understanding also in future cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll do my best. It's a relatively long process in respect of the development of translations related to intercepts. The intercepts, and you'll see this in some of the 92 bis applications and other evidence from live witnesses as well, were generally recorded in the context of the ABiH 2nd Corps intercepts. They were generally recorded, written down on note-books. So the handwritten document that you've seen in e-court is from a note-book that the intercept operator actually wrote down the conversation that he listened to. The process, as you'll come to know, involves -- once the operator has written that down, that handwritten note-book gets sent over to another individual, who then types down what is written in the handwritten document and generates a printed version of this intercept. That printed version that gets transmitted from the location where the intercepts are actually first taken down to another office where they are analysed. In some instances, the received printed intercept is then analysed and put together with other intercepts, which generates yet another version of a typewritten print-out. All of those documents are then -- are also, I should say, encoded in computer. They are written on a, for example, a word-processing document and stored electronically. Those stored electronic versions were also received by the Prosecution. And in some instances, because they were electronic, they could be printed directly, and so they weren't photocopied. So when I say we had not so good printed version of the intercept, those refer to those photocopied versions that came from another office outside of where the original intercepts were transcribed and typed. Then we also received the electronic versions of those intercepts, the ones that were actually encoded, written into a word-processing document, which we could print out. Those documents are much clearer, obviously, because they are first-generation print. They're not photocopied or anything. So that accounts for the different versions of the B/C/S intercepts. And then we have situations where the photocopied version, versus the -- photocopied typewritten versions, versus the first-generation printed version from the electronic format, have been transcribed -- have been interpreted, sometimes differently, because they're done at different times by different people, and sometimes differently because there are defects, shall we say, on the photocopied version; a word isn't clear because the photocopy didn't come out properly. So, for example, in the intercept that we just saw on the screen, where you see the slash lines with "passage missing," you may see that in respect of the poorly photocopied versions, because the photocopy didn't come out properly and the text is literally not -- can't be seen on that bad photocopy. On the first-generation printed electronic version, the text is clearly there because it's not photocopied. It's essentially a very clear image. And that accounts for some of the differences in the translation of those texts. So that's the reason why we have, I think in a nutshell, a number of different versions of them, and occasionally we'll see slight differences -- you will see slight differences between what's in the handwritten text and what's in the typewritten text on relatively minor issues, such as the time. As I indicated in the one we just saw, the handwritten version reads "at 1132," the typewritten -- well, in this case the translation that you could see indicated "1135." That's based on the typewritten version of this very same intercept. Textually, they are indistinguishable substantively. That's all I can tell you for the moment. You'll hear more from the operators when they get here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just another to that from Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the explanation. Does that also account for what you referred to in line 17, page 37, regarding the language -- English language? You said that -- where are we? You seem to imply -- yes. I just need to understand whether the process you have explained, which I understand, also relates to the language of translation. You say in line 17, The number of the English translation is so-and-so, the other English translation - this is line 25 - is 3142D. Are you referring to one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When I say the other English translation, I'm saying the other English translation of the same B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so they are two different versions of that B/C/S document, two different translations of that B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So, in other words, the same document has been translated twice, and you would have two different versions of one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see your question. Well, no. Sometimes that happens, I have to be honest, but in this particular instance I'm talking about two different translations of two different documents. One is a translation of the handwritten document, and the other is a translation of the typewritten document. And what you saw on the screen was a translation of the typewritten document while we were looking at the handwritten document. And so when I was questioning the witness, I was reading from a translation of the handwritten document and mistakenly a translation of the typewritten document was before the Court in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So I'm tendering all of them, so that we can clear on what is what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I take it the typewritten document was taken from the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The typewritten document -- the handwritten document is what the intercept writer -- intercept operator transcribes when he listens to the conversation. And then that handwritten document is given over to a typist, who types the document and sends it for further consideration to other organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He types it from the handwritten?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A handwritten note-book?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And not from the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Not from the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So he's listening again to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. On occasion, and you'll hear more from the intercept operators, but on occasion they do collaborate, they sit together, they listen to the tapes, in order to resolve certain ambiguities or difficult passages to hear. But then it goes to the typist, or encryption person, who then types down what's written and sends that. So there's a typed version of the handwritten document which, I would say, 90 per cent of the time, 99 per cent of the time, corresponds identically to the handwritten version, but occasionally you see discrepancies, as you see in this case, "1132" on the handwritten, "1135" on the translation on the translation of the typewritten document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. I think that helps also for future instances. Thank you very much again. And I take it you've finished your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have now the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since Mr. Vanderpuye announced that they have around 300 transcripts to offer in this case, and we heard what he said: "Some were interpreted in a different way, some documents like this original ..." et cetera. Some are typed, some are print-outs. I kindly ask you that all transcripts they want to tender in this case be subjected to expertise before the testimony of operators, and not admit transcripts then. Because Mr. Vanderpuye just said that 90 per cent of the transcripts are accurate and 10 are not. One of you Judges also noticed the same thing. Please decide who will review these transcripts by the Defence and by the Prosecution, and submit them to an expert, only those that will be admitted in this case, because I read in earlier cases, such as Popovic et al -- I saw that they are differently interpreted, these transcripts, these intercepts, in different translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think the Chamber has to consider your application. We will come back to that later. And now I think it's time for continuing the examination of this witness. But I think you are on your feet, Mr. Vanderpuye. You want to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I only wanted to point out that - and I'm sure Mr. Tolimir is aware, as Mr. Gajic is - these intercepts, the ones that we are tendering or intend to tender in this case, have been admitted and vetted in a number of trials. And I'm sure Mr. Tolimir is aware, as he says, that there are differences in some of these translations, and that's simply a human factor. Different people translate things differently, even though they are equally qualified to do so. And, clearly, if he has an issue with respect to any given translation, there's nothing that prevents him from challenging it or having it translated for his own purposes, provided he has the resources to do so. And I think that's about all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As I indicated already, Mr. Tolimir, we will take into consideration your concern, and now we should continue with the examination of the witness. You have your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to continue. I would just like to say one simple sentence. I'm not asking for a verification of the translations. I just would like to see the original in the note-book, where the intercept is written in the original handwriting. I'm not going to pursue this. I would just like to be able to see that before using the translation that is being used today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we had the original note-book on the screen before us. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for sometimes being very persistent, but I did participate in the verification of documents. We didn't have the entire note-book. We only looked at one page, and it could have been created the day before. So, anyway, I would like to say hello to the witness, that I hope that the proceedings will not be completed according to my will, but according to the will of the Lord. So I would like to refer him now to his statement, on page 4, lines 1, 2, 3 and 4, in the Serbian language. It's the last page in the Serbian, and it's the last page of the document in the English. These are the last lines, last eight lines. Thank you. I apologise. My legal advisor is telling me that it's page 3 in the English translation. Thank you. We can see page 1 on the screen in the Serbian. Can we look at page 4 in the Serbian, please, lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. All right, it's marked. Can you please zoom in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you please look at this second sentence at the beginning of this page. I'm going to quote what you said, and then I will put a question to you: "I do not recall any conversation with Rubez regarding Himzo Mujic. I also don't remember any conversation regarding Himzo Mujic conducted with my former chief, Goran Kanostrevac. "I heard that there was a military prison in Vlasenica known as Susica, but I do not recall the time-period. I have never been there, and I had no contacts with the prison wardens." And we're going to wait for the interpreters to interpret this, and then my question will be -- thank you. Witness, sir, are these your words that I have just read from your statement that you provided on the 17th of March, 2008, which is a Prosecution document P161? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Since you don't recall anything that refers to this conversation from this transcript, that you said anything like this any time, I'm going to ask you this: The contents of this transcript, is that something that you found out only when you spoke with them on the 17th of March, 2011 -- 2008?

utterances.speaker: NIKODIN JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for this witness. I would like to thank you, and I would like to wish the witness a safe journey home, and I am thanking him for coming to this Tribunal to testify and for having confirmed his prior statement and his prior testimony. Thank you very much. Safe trip, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicic, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination. Thank you very much for your attendance here in The Hague again, and you are free now to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much, and the Court Officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I suppose we have another witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry, I forgot to update you. I've spoken with my colleague, and we have essentially agreed that Mr. Janc should testify now. And I believe they will attempt to begin their cross-examination sometime tomorrow and, if unable to complete it, complete it sometime after the testimony of the following witness. And if that's all right with the Court, I think we are prepared to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Welcome back to the Tribunal, this trial, Mr. Janc. May I remind you that the affirmation that you made to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution has some more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know that you've already testified to some extent already in this case, so I won't go into your background. But in the context of your function as an OTP investigator, have you had any involvement in reviewing the evidence that is related to the number of victims concerning Srebrenica and Zepa events?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did your involvement in this area of the investigation begin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say towards the end of 2007, when Dean Manning was here preparing for his testimony in Popovic and -- in the Popovic case. And then particularly for his purposes, I went on a mission to visit all the sites -- the exhumation sites in Bosnia and Herzegovina related to Srebrenica events, and so that was in October 2007. And from then on, I was constantly involved in the exhumations of the Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
